ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Hepatology Referral — Ernest Hemingway — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Establishing primary care: heavy drinking, low mood and forgetfulness a year after two plane crashes, with high blood pressure and abnormal liver and iron tests on the intake panel

text.paragraph: Raised transferrin saturation and ferritin with raised liver enzymes in a 55-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder. Please advise on the cause, whether and how to stage his liver, and treatment. [S]
Urgency: Within two weeks, on the same day as his two-week primary care visit. [S]

list.item: If the HFE test shows hemochromatosis, how much of the iron overload is genetic and how much is due to alcohol?
Does his liver need staging, and can this be done without a biopsy?
What phlebotomy schedule and ferritin target do you advise?
Is naltrexone safe for his liver, and what should we tell him about alcohol?
Does he need liver cancer surveillance, and what should his relatives and his diet do?

text.paragraph: Writer, about ten drinks a day for many years (AUDIT 26), no withdrawal seizures or delirium, never treated. Concussion with a skull fracture and injuries to the right kidney, liver and spleen in two plane crashes a year ago. Today's tests: transferrin saturation 76%, ferritin 1,460 ng/mL, serum iron 214 ug/dL; AST 70, ALT 78 and GGT 196 U/L; bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL, albumin 4.1 g/dL, platelets 208; MCV 102 fL; HbA1c 6.1%; triglycerides 236 mg/dL. HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C tests nonreactive. Blood pressure 152/94. PHQ-9 16 with passive thoughts of death and no intent or plan; a safety plan is in place. HFE genotyping sent today. Started today: naltrexone 50 mg daily for a goal of cutting down that he chose, thiamine, sertraline 50 mg and amlodipine 5 mg. He takes no supplements [S]

list.item: He is afraid of losing his memory and his ability to write. [S]
He wants to drink less without being told he must never drink again. [S]
He worries about headaches and pain since the crashes. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Ernest Hemingway was born on July 21, 1899, in Oak Park, Illinois, the son of a physician. [D]

In the First World War he joined a volunteer ambulance unit in the Italian army; in 1918 he was wounded at the front near Fossalta di Piave by a mortar shell, was decorated by the Italian government, and spent a long time in hospitals. [D]
He drank heavily for most of his adult life. [D]

In January 1954, on a safari in Africa, he survived two plane crashes on consecutive days in Uganda. In the second he forced a jammed door open with his head and suffered a concussion and a skull fracture; he also reported a ruptured right kidney and injuries to his liver and spleen. The Nobel Prize biography records that the accidents caused severe pain for the rest of his life. [D]
He was awarded the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature and could not attend the ceremony in Stockholm because of ill health. [D]
His home from 1939 to 1960 was Finca Vigía, a farm on a hillside outside Havana, Cuba, where he wrote much of his work. [D]
His father, a physician who was described as depressed and diabetic, died by suicide in 1928. [D]
Several earlier members of his family also had depression and died by suicide, and he understood himself to be descended from men who had died by suicide on both sides of his family. [D]

text.paragraph: 8 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.

list.item: Alcohol use disorder, severe; heavy daily drinking for most of his adult life; synthetic modern episode linked to his documented heavy drinking: active, confirmed [S]
Raised transferrin saturation and ferritin found on routine intake tests, cause not yet known (heavy drinking, liver disease or iron overload): active, confirmed [S]
Major depressive disorder, single episode, moderate; Mood Disorder Questionnaire negative and no history of mania or hypomania: active, confirmed [S]
Essential hypertension, stage 2, with heavy drinking contributing: active, confirmed [S]

Post-concussion symptoms (headaches, slowed thinking and forgetfulness) after repeated head injuries, most recently a concussion with a skull fracture a year ago; chronic traumatic encephalopathy is not diagnosed: active, confirmed [S]
Prediabetes (HbA1c 6.1%): active, confirmed [S]

Alcohol: AUDIT and DSM-5-TR assessment, brief intervention in his own terms, naltrexone 50 mg daily, thiamine, a drinking diary, a goal he chooses and revisits, withdrawal precautions if he stops (no abrupt stop at his intake level without a plan), and mutual-help or counseling options offered. Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients With Alcohol Use Disorder (2018); The ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management (2020); Unhealthy Alcohol Use in Adolescents and Adults: Screening and Behavioral Counseling Interventions (2018) [S]

Depression: PHQ-9 at each visit, weekly psychotherapy (cognitive behavioral therapy) with the clinic's behavioral health clinician, sertraline, the Mood Disorder Questionnaire before the antidepressant, a structured safety assessment with a written safety plan, lethal-means counseling about firearms, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and safety review at every visit. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hypertension and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026) [S]

Post-concussion symptoms: symptom-based care (headache plan without daily analgesics, sleep routine, graded activity, writing in shorter sessions), MoCA repeated after three months with less alcohol, no routine brain imaging without warning signs, and neuropsychological testing if thinking does not improve; chronic traumatic encephalopathy not diagnosed. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management and Rehabilitation of Post-Acute Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (2021) [S]

Hypertension: home blood pressure monitoring, amlodipine, less alcohol and salt, ECG and urine albumin at diagnosis, echocardiogram for stage 2 hypertension, and a target below 130/80 mmHg. Guideline: 2017 ACC/AHA/AAPA/ABC/ACPM/AGS/APhA/ASH/ASPC/NMA/PCNA Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2017); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hypertension and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026) [S]

Prediabetes: HbA1c repeated at six months, less alcohol, activity and diet; iron overload and alcohol both raise the risk of diabetes. Guideline: ACG Clinical Guideline: Hereditary Hemochromatosis (2019); Prediabetes and Type 2 Diabetes: Screening (2021) [S]
Referral to hepatology, Ingrid Solheim, MD, ordered 1955-03-02 [S]
